issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing re-investigation and retrial of the same offence on the same set of facts, after having held that the appellant deserved acquittal.

facts: The appellant was initially convicted by a Trial Court.
On appeal, the High Court acquitted the appellant.
In the same judgment where it acquitted the appellant, the High Court directed a 'de novo' (new) investigation by the CBI into the same offense based on the same set of facts.
Following this new investigation, a new chargesheet was filed against the appellant, leading to a new trial.
The appellant challenged this new proceeding, arguing it constituted a retrial for an offense for which he had already been acquitted.
law: Article 20(2) of the Constitution of India and Section 300 of the Cr.P.C. establish the principle of 'double jeopardy', which prohibits a person from being prosecuted and punished for the same offense more than once.
Section 386 of the Cr.P.C. grants appellate courts the power to order a 'retrial', but it does not explicitly provide for 're-investigation'.

Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. allows for 'further investigation' with a magistrate's permission, but not a complete 're-investigation' from scratch, which is a concept invoked only in exceptional circumstances.

For the principle of double jeopardy to apply, three conditions must be met: (1) a person must have been prosecuted by a competent court, (2) the proceeding must have resulted in a conviction or acquittal that is currently in force, and (3) the new proceeding must be for the same offense.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's order was for a 're-investigation', not merely a 'retrial' or 'further investigation'.
The Court then applied the three conditions for double jeopardy to the case:
1. The first condition was met because the appellant had been prosecuted and convicted by the Trial Court, which was a competent court.
2. The second condition was met because the High Court's acquittal was a final order that remained in force.

3. The third condition was also met. The Court reasoned that since the High Court ordered a completely new investigation by a different agency (CBI), the process had to 'begin from zero'. This new investigation, new chargesheet, and new examination of witnesses constituted a second, separate prosecution for the same offense, unlike a retrial which is considered a continuation of the original trial.
Therefore, the Court determined that ordering a fresh investigation after the appellant had already been acquitted violated the constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in directing a re-investigation and retrial. Ordering a new investigation on the same facts after acquitting the appellant was impermissible and violated the appellant's fundamental right against double jeopardy under Article 20(2) of the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in directing re-investigation and retrial of the same offence on the same set of facts, after having held that the appellant deserved acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The direction to conduct a de novo investigation by the CBI is being challenged.
An acquittal should be considered 'honorable' and a full exoneration when the prosecution completely fails to prove its case, making a retrial inappropriate.
The re-investigation and retrial violate the appellant's constitutional right against double jeopardy under Article 20(2) of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's challenge to the proceedings was belated. They only approached the High Court after 34 prosecution witnesses were examined and they realized there was sufficient evidence for a conviction.
The case is special and exemplary, making a retrial inevitable and necessary to prevent the recurrence of such an event.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person's right under Article 20(2) of the Constitution, which protects against being prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once, is violated by subsequent proceedings for that same offence.
obiter: The principle that an accused is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt cannot be sacrificed due to inefficiency, inadequacy, or inept handling of an investigation.
The principle against double jeopardy is also recognized in Section 26 of the General Clauses Act and Section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The Fifth Amendment of the American Constitution enunciates the principle against double jeopardy.
It is normally for the appellate court to decide whether to adjudicate by taking into account additional evidence or to direct a fresh trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: This Court is of the view that the right enshrined in Article 20(2) of the appellant stands violated. The vision of the High Court, in our considered view was bad in law, and is therefore quashed and set aside. All proceedings subsequent to such direction, necessarily have to be held as such and therefore quashed and set aside as well.
legal_tests_applied: The constitutional protection against double jeopardy under Article 20(2).

The conditions under which a retrial can be ordered, such as when the original trial court lacked jurisdiction or the trial was vitiated by a fundamental illegality or irregularity based on a misconception of the proceedings.
policy_considerations: The principle that an accused is presumed to be innocent till he is proved guilty beyond a reasonable doubt cannot be sacrificed on the altar of inefficiency, inadequacy or inept handling of the investigation.

If the CBI were to be involved in numerous cases due to flawed local investigations, it would be flooded with a large number of cases and, with limited resources, may find it difficult to properly investigate even serious cases, thereby losing its credibility and purpose.
